extracted.intended_audience: aspiring poets, literary students, and readers of literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and critical observations about choosing a subject for a long descriptive-reflective poem and how to compose it so parts cohere — covering subject choice, balance of description/incident/reflection, observational practice, and the importance of unity and smooth transitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject that gives equal room to modes and supplies unity
rubrics_metrics.description: “I sought for a subject, that should give equal room and freedom for description, incident, and impassioned reflections on men, nature, and society, yet supply in itself a natural connexion to the parts, and unity to the whole.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a subject intrinsically capacious enough to accommodate varied elements (description, incident, reflection) while itself providing the natural connective tissue and unity for the piece. Example given: tracing a stream from source to sea as a subject that affords description, incident, and reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carry the titular subject through the work
rubrics_metrics.description: “the subject, which gives the title to the work, was not, and indeed could not be, carried on beyond the three or four first pages...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid making the title-subject a mere framing device that disappears after the opening. A defect is when the named subject appears only briefly and then the poem wanders; ensure the central subject recurs or remains operative throughout to maintain coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure natural connexions between parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism: “throughout the poem, the connexions are frequently awkward, and the transitions abrupt and arbitrary.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work to create organic links between sections; connections should feel natural rather than forced. Abrupt, arbitrary transitions are an anti-pattern — aim for logical or image-based bridges that flow from one part to the next.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance description, incident, and impassioned reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: “equal room and freedom for description, incident, and impassioned reflections on men, nature, and society”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the poem so it can accommodate evocative descriptive passages, narrative/incident, and argumentative or emotional reflection in roughly balanced measure when that balance suits the work’s aims; neglecting one mode can make the poem feel lopsided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work from immediate observation and make studies
rubrics_metrics.description: “With my pencil and memorandum book in my hand, I was making stud[ies] as the artists call them, and often moulding my thoughts into verse, with the objects and imagery immediately before my senses.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use on-site observation and sketching/memoranda while walking or experiencing the landscape; mould thoughts into verse from direct sensory input. Practical technique: daily walks, pencil and memorandum book, composing lines while the imagery is present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select a subject that naturally unites varied parts (example: the stream)
rubrics_metrics.description: The author’s chosen model-subject: a stream 'traced from its source in the hills ... to the first break or fall ... to the peat and turf barn ... to the hamlet, the villages, the market-town, the manufactories, and the sea-port.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete, processual subjects (e.g., a brook/stream) that naturally permit progression and linkage of episodes and scenes, giving descriptive freedom while providing a built-in narrative/structural arc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground writing in principles for enduring value
rubrics_metrics.description: Observing Edmund Burke: 'He referred habitually to principles. He was a scientific statesman; and therefore a seer. For every principle contains in itself the germ of a prophecy...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anchor essays or political/literary arguments in clear, general principles; such principled grounding produces foresight and gives the writing lasting interest beyond immediate circumstances. In other words, work that explicates or is organized around durable principles will age better.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistence, refinement, and depth matter even if uncomfortable
rubrics_metrics.description: “Wearisome as Burke's refinements appeared to his parliamentary auditors, yet the cultivated classes throughout Europe have reason to be thankful, that he went on refining.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not shy from refinement and intellectual depth because they may seem tedious to some contemporaries; careful refinement can be the source of a work’s long-term value. Anti-pattern: abandoning careful refinement to seek immediate popularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enrich poetic practice by study of ethics and psychology
rubrics_metrics.description: The author devoted himself 'to poetry and to the study of ethics and psychology' during his retirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broaden intellectual resources (e.g., ethics, psychology) to deepen thematic complexity and human insight in poetry. Such study can inform reflections and moral/philosophical dimensions of verse.
